row.title: How The Beggars Came To Town
row.author: L Frank Baum

plot_extraction.response_text:
Twelve-year-old Prince Lilimond learns that beggars throughout his father’s prosperous kingdom claim to be starving because of royal taxes. When the King dismisses his concerns, Lilimond uses a promised birthday wish to request absolute rule for one day. He plans to distribute a gold piece to every beggar and summons them from across the kingdom.

On the appointed day, so many people gather that the treasury cannot provide gold for everyone. Advised by the Chamberlain, Lilimond examines each claimant individually and discovers that many are healthy idlers, wealthy opportunists, or outright frauds. After he threatens punishment for deception, the impostors flee, leaving only a small number of genuinely needy people, who receive aid from a fraction of one royal coffer.

Realizing that not everyone who begs is truly destitute, Lilimond acknowledges that he misjudged his father’s councilors and returns the crown before his day of rule ends. He later becomes King after his father’s death, having learned to combine compassion with careful judgment.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the style of a traditional literary fairy tale or moral fable, combining courtly fantasy with explicit social instruction. Its setting is an idealized, vaguely medieval monarchy of thrones, heralds, coffers, tourneys, velvet garments, and royal proclamations. The opening nursery rhyme establishes a folkloric frame and introduces the central motif of beggars in “rags,” “tags,” and “velvet gown,” categories that the subsequent plot literalizes. The tale then proceeds in a clear, linear sequence: the compassionate prince identifies an apparent injustice, obtains temporary power to remedy it, encounters practical complications, and emerges with a revised moral understanding.

The narrative voice is third-person omniscient, confident, and openly evaluative. It moves freely between outward action, characters’ thoughts, and broad claims about human behavior. The narrator labels figures as tender-hearted, wise, lazy, greedy, deserving, or fraudulent rather than leaving such judgments entirely to the reader. Occasional direct addresses and proverbial observations—especially in the closing paragraphs—give the voice the quality of an adult storyteller instructing a younger audience. The ending makes the lesson explicit, interpreting the events and appealing to the maxim that it is “better to give than to receive.”

The diction is formal, courtly, and deliberately archaic. Expressions such as “methinks,” “of a surety,” “sire,” “hath,” “whatsoever,” “succor,” “alms,” and “so be it” create an old-world atmosphere, while titles and honorifics are repeatedly capitalized to emphasize hierarchy and ceremony. Dialogue is highly polished and rhetorical even when spoken by a twelve-year-old. Characters address one another through elaborate formulas—“Your Majesty,” “oh sire,” and “my King”—and often express arguments in balanced, carefully reasoned sentences. This makes conversation serve less as naturalistic speech than as a vehicle for debating charity, taxation, authority, and social responsibility.

The prose alternates between extended descriptive or explanatory passages and long scenes of dialogue. Sentences are often compound or complex, joined by semicolons and coordinating conjunctions, with periodic inversions such as “Very fair and sweet was little Prince Lilimond” and “Then did the Prince command.” Repetition supplies emphasis and a storybook rhythm: the King repeatedly cries “Nonsense!”, beggars arrive “singly and by twos and threes,” and the crowd is evoked through the “tramp, tramp” of feet and the barking of dogs. Formulaic transitions—“Then said,” “Now this Borland,” “And so,” and “Thus ended”—reinforce the oral-tale quality and keep the narrative easy to follow.

Characterization is broad and functional. Lilimond is initially defined by beauty, courtesy, compassion, and youthful idealism; the King by affection, complacency, and attachment to courtly pleasures; Borland by kindness without worldly judgment; and the royal officials by administrative caution. Characters chiefly embody positions in a moral argument rather than possessing deep psychological complexity. Physical details are symbolic and readily legible: rags, infirmity, velvet, rings, and silver buckles become signs by which need or deception is judged. The story’s central contrast is therefore between appearance and reality, particularly between being a beggar and being genuinely destitute.

The tone is genial, decorous, and didactic, with mild humor and irony. The prince’s noble plan appears destined for heroic success, but the crowd includes wealthy opportunists and able-bodied idlers, overturning his assumptions. The irony is gentle rather than cruel: Lilimond’s mistake arises from excessive compassion, and his brief reign functions as an educational trial. Suspense is modest and depends on whether the treasury will be emptied and whether the inexperienced child can distinguish legitimate need from fraud.

Structurally, the tale relies on symmetry and reversal. Lilimond begins by distrusting the King’s councilors and believing that widespread begging proves widespread starvation; after exercising power himself, he accepts the councilors’ wisdom and restores the crown before sunset. The one-day reign acts as a contained moral experiment. Concrete recurring images—the crown, scepter, treasury, gold pieces, clothing, and barking dogs—bind the political lesson to recognizable fairy-tale objects.

The governing style is overtly moralistic and socially conservative. It praises compassion and aid for the genuinely needy but distrusts indiscriminate charity, presenting many claimants as lazy or fraudulent and ultimately affirming the existing monarchy as prosperous and just. Rather than exposing structural injustice, the conclusion narrows the problem to discerning individual worthiness. The resulting profile is that of an accessible children’s court tale: ornamental but lucid, dialogue-driven, proverb-like in its reasoning, gently ironic in development, and explicit in its final moral.

## Prince Lilimond’s Day of Rule

> Beggars in tatters, beggars in tags,  
> Beggars who flourish in velvet and rags;  
> Some cry for supper, and some cry for gold—  
> Look twice, little Prince, ere thy treasure be told.

Very fair and sweet was little Prince Lilimond, only son of King Florimund, who ruled over the pleasant kingdom of Valedore. His hair was yellow as ripe corn in the sunlight, his eyes were blue as the flowers that grow beside a brook, and his manners were so courteous that the oldest Duke in the realm declared he had never known the Prince to forget either a title or a kindness.

But that which was best in Lilimond was his tender heart. He could not see a lame dog without desiring to carry it home, nor hear that a woodcutter’s cottage had burned without sending his own blankets to the family. If a page cut his finger, Lilimond fetched the salve; if an old soldier stood bareheaded in the snow, the Prince would remove his own fur cap and thrust it upon the veteran.

Now a tender heart is a noble possession; yet, like a fine horse, it must be guided by judgment, lest it carry its owner into a ditch.

Valedore was a prosperous kingdom. Its wheat fields rolled golden from hill to hill; its orchards were rosy with apples; its rivers turned many mills, and merchants came from distant countries to buy the silks, wines, clocks, and carved chests made by the King’s subjects. The roads were well kept, robbers were scarce, and even the poorest village had a fountain and a bell.

King Florimund was not unkind. He loved justice, good dinners, hawking, tourneys, bright banners, and long evenings when minstrels sang before the fire. He left much of the business of government to his councilors, who were grave men in robes of crimson and black. Because the kingdom flourished, the King believed that all was as it should be.

One autumn morning Prince Lilimond rode out with his tutor, Master Borland. Now this Borland was a learned and gentle man, who could speak seven languages, name every star in the northern sky, and write a poem upon any subject from roses to rhinoceroses. Yet he knew little of cheats, idlers, or crafty persons, for he supposed that every man’s heart was as honest as his own.

As they passed through the eastern gate, an old beggar stretched forth a trembling hand.

“Alms, noble Prince!” he cried. “Have pity upon one who hath not tasted bread since yesterday. The royal taxes have taken my last penny.”

Lilimond gave him the silver clasp from his cloak.

A little farther on, a woman in a torn gray shawl sat beside the road with two children.

“Succor us, gracious lord,” she wailed. “We starve beneath the burden of the King’s taxes.”

The Prince emptied his purse into her lap.

Before noon he had heard the same complaint from a blind fiddler, a man with a bandaged foot, three barefoot boys, two bent old women, and a fellow who carried a sleeping infant and wept so loudly that the infant awoke and wept also.

At last Lilimond turned a troubled face toward his tutor.

“Master Borland,” said he, “can it be true that my father’s people starve?”

“Methinks it must be true if so many declare it,” replied Borland sadly. “For although one tongue may lie, surely twenty tongues cannot all lie together.”

This sounded reasonable to the Prince, though it was not so reasonable as it sounded.

When Lilimond returned to the palace, he went straight to the Great Hall. There sat King Florimund beneath a canopy of cloth-of-gold, listening while the Master of Revels described a tournament that was to be held upon the Prince’s twelfth birthday.

“Father,” cried Lilimond, forgetting ceremony in his distress, “the people are starving!”

The King raised his eyebrows.

“Which people?”

“The people of Valedore, sire. I have seen beggars at the gate and upon the roads. They say that your taxes have taken their bread.”

“Nonsense!” said the King.

“They were dressed in rags.”

“Rags may be put on as easily as velvet.”

“One man was blind.”

“He may have been blind,” said the King, “but blindness doth not prove that my taxes caused it.”

“There was a poor woman with hungry children.”

“Were they hungry?”

“They said so.”

“Nonsense!” repeated the King, though not angrily. “Valedore’s taxes are lighter than those of any neighboring realm, and no man unable to labor is refused bread at the parish house. My councilors have examined these matters.”

“Your councilors sit upon cushioned chairs,” said Lilimond, with more courage than courtesy. “They do not hear the cries outside the gate.”

At this the Lord Treasurer frowned, the Chancellor coughed behind his hand, and the First Chamberlain looked at the painted ceiling. But the King loved his son and forgave him.

“My dear child,” said he, “when thou art older, thou wilt learn that a kingdom cannot be governed by every cry heard beside a highway. Some complain because they suffer; others complain because complaint is easier than work.”

“But if there be even one who suffers through us, should we not help him?”

“Of a surety. Yet help given foolishly may feed dishonesty and leave honesty hungry.”

Lilimond shook his head.

“It seemeth to me, sire, that gold is plentiful in the palace, while misery is plentiful beyond it.”

“Nonsense!” cried the King for the third time. “Come, let us speak of thy birthday. Thou shalt be twelve years old next Thursday, and I have promised thee whatsoever gift thou desirest, provided it be within my power and contrary neither to honor nor law. Wouldst thou have a white charger? A jeweled sword? A ship with purple sails?”

Then a bold idea entered Lilimond’s mind.

“My father,” said he, kneeling before the throne, “I ask neither horse, sword, nor ship. Grant me instead the government of Valedore for one day, with power to command whatsoever even the King might command.”

A whisper ran through the court.

The Lord Treasurer dropped his ivory counting rod. The Chancellor said, “Your Majesty!” in a voice of alarm, and the Queen’s ladies fluttered like startled pigeons.

King Florimund looked long at his son.

“That is a grave gift for a child.”

“You gave your royal promise, sire.”

“So I did,” said the King; for kings, above all men, must keep their promises. “Thou shalt rule from sunrise until sunset upon thy birthday. Yet remember, Lilimond: a crown is heavier than it appears when lying upon velvet.”

“I shall remember,” replied the Prince, though in truth he thought chiefly of the good he would accomplish.

All that week he and Master Borland made their plans. They counted villages upon maps, consulted tables of population, and calculated the number of poor persons likely to require aid. Borland, who trusted every written figure and every spoken lament, concluded that one large coffer of gold would suffice.

Then did the Prince command heralds to ride throughout Valedore and make this proclamation:

“Hear ye! Hear ye! Upon the twelfth birthday of His Highness Prince Lilimond, every beggar who presents himself at the Royal Palace before noon shall receive one piece of gold, enough to buy bread for many weeks. Let none who suffer hunger fail to come!”

The heralds blew silver trumpets in market squares, beside village wells, before monastery gates, and at lonely crossroads. The news flew faster than the heralds. Peddlers carried it over the hills; boatmen shouted it along the rivers; shepherds repeated it from one valley to the next.

And wherever the news went, men began to reckon.

“A gold piece for asking!” said some. “Why should we not ask?”

Thursday dawned clear and cold. Before the sun had wholly risen, bells rang from every tower of the palace. The King entered the throne room wearing his crown and carrying the scepter of Valedore. Courtiers, ministers, captains, and judges stood in two glittering rows.

Prince Lilimond came forward in white satin and a mantle of blue velvet. He was pale with solemnity, but his eyes shone.

King Florimund removed the crown from his own head and placed it upon the boy’s golden hair. It slipped down over one eyebrow, and a page had to fit a small cushion beneath it; nevertheless, no one smiled.

“From sunrise until sunset,” proclaimed the King, “Lilimond is ruler of Valedore. His word shall be obeyed as mine.”

“Long live King Lilimond!” cried the court.

The boy seated himself upon the throne, and King Florimund took a plain chair at his right hand.

“Open the palace gates,” commanded Lilimond. “Bring forth the gold, and let every beggar receive his piece.”

The First Chamberlain bowed, but he did not move.

“Your Majesty,” said he, “I beg leave to report that there is some difficulty outside.”

“What difficulty can there be?”

“The multitude is greater than was expected.”

“How many have come?”

“It cannot easily be counted, sire.”

“Then look from the western balcony,” said King Florimund quietly.

Lilimond went to the balcony, followed by Borland, the Chamberlain, and half the court.

Never had he beheld such a sight.

The great square was filled from wall to wall. People crowded the steps, the fountains, and the roofs of nearby houses. Beyond the square, the road appeared black with newcomers. They came singly and by twos and threes; they came in families, companies, and entire wagonloads. There were men on crutches, women carrying babies, boys with torn caps, old soldiers, barefoot girls, blind fiddlers, traveling tinkers, fortune-tellers, laborers, and persons of no occupation that any man could name.

Tramp, tramp, tramp came the feet upon the road. Babies cried, donkeys brayed, and dogs barked until the bronze lions over the gate seemed ready to bark in answer.

Lilimond’s joy gave way to astonishment.

“Are all these people starving?”

“So they declare,” said Borland, though less confidently than before.

The Lord Treasurer approached, looking whiter than his parchment collar.

“Your Majesty, the first coffer hath been brought forth, and six others stand ready. Yet if each person in that square receives one gold piece, seven coffers will not suffice, nor seventy. We should empty the treasury before the rear of the procession entered the city.”

“Then empty it,” said Lilimond, gripping the scepter. “I have promised.”

The Treasurer looked as though a sword had pierced him.

“Sire, without gold we cannot pay the guards who defend the borders, repair the bridges, purchase grain in a season of famine, or maintain the hospitals and parish houses. To relieve one day’s petitioners, Your Majesty would imperil the whole kingdom.”

Lilimond’s face grew red.

“Shall I break my word?”

The First Chamberlain bent low. He was an elderly man named Lord Ardwell, whose silver buckles were always polished and whose mind was even more orderly than his garments.

“May it please Your Majesty,” said he, “your proclamation promised gold to every beggar. It did not promise gold to every person who chose to dress as one. Examine the claimants, sire, and give to those whose need is true.”

“Would that not be cruel delay?”

“It is not cruelty to separate want from greed. Indeed, it is mercy; for whatsoever gold is taken by a deceiver cannot be given to an honest sufferer.”

The words were much like those King Florimund had spoken, but Lilimond was now upon the throne, and advice sounds different when one must answer for the result.

“So be it,” he said. “Bring the claimants into the Hall of Judgment, one at a time.”

The first was a huge fellow in a torn brown cloak. His cheeks were ruddy, his shoulders broad, and his hands smooth and strong.

“Why dost thou beg?” asked Lilimond.

“Because I am too weak to labor, my King,” groaned the man, leaning heavily upon a stick.

Lord Ardwell dropped a silver coin beside him.

The man stooped and snatched it up before it ceased ringing.

“Thou art quick for one so weak,” observed the Prince.

“My weakness comes and goes, sire.”

“What labor hast thou sought?”

“None, Your Majesty. Labor would worsen my condition.”

A murmur of laughter passed through the court.

“Take him to the palace garden,” said Lilimond, “and let him weed one bed. If he cannot do it, he shall receive gold and food. If he can, he shall be offered honest work.”

At once the fellow threw away his stick and fled so swiftly that two guards could scarcely open the door in time.

The second claimant was a woman wrapped in patched shawls. She bent almost double and spoke in a cracked whisper.

“Pity a poor widow, gracious King. I possess nothing in this world.”

As she bowed, a pearl necklace slipped from beneath her shawl.

“Nothing save pearls,” said Lilimond.

The woman clutched the necklace.

“They are but glass, sire.”

The royal jeweler examined them.

“Orient pearls of excellent quality, Your Majesty. Worth three hundred pieces of gold.”

Then the woman straightened; and all perceived that she was neither old nor bent, but the prosperous wife of a merchant.

“I meant no harm,” she cried. “I thought that since Your Majesty intended to give gold away, one piece more or less could matter little.”

“One drop matters little,” answered Lilimond, “yet enough drops will drain a fountain. Go, and be ashamed.”

The merchant’s wife departed with her shawl drawn over her face.

Next came a man with both eyes bandaged.

“Alas!” he moaned. “I have been blind from birth.”

“Then how didst thou find thy way from thy village?” asked the Prince.

“My faithful dog guided me.”

At that moment a palace hound wandered near. The man leaped upon a bench and shouted, “Keep that beast from me!”

“How knewest thou it was a beast?” asked Lilimond.

The man tore off his bandages and ran.

After him appeared six boys who claimed to be orphans. Upon questioning, it was discovered that they all had living fathers and mothers and had been promised sweet cakes by an alehouse keeper if they returned with gold. Then came a stout farmer wearing rags over his good woolen clothes; a tailor who had sewn patches upon a new coat that very morning; and a young nobleman disguised with soot, who wished to win a wager from his companions.

The Prince ordered the soot washed from the young nobleman’s face, whereupon three Lords recognized their nephew. Their indignation was great, though not so great as his embarrassment.

Hour followed hour. The crowd outside still roared, shuffled, whistled, quarreled, ate sausages, and complained of delay.

Some claimants were poor indeed, but not helpless. To these Lilimond offered work upon royal roads, in orchards, kitchens, stables, and workshops. Many accepted gladly. Others became angry.

“I came for gold, not work,” said one.

“Then thou camest for treasure rather than succor,” replied the Prince. “There shall be no gold for thee.”

Shortly before noon, Lord Ardwell whispered, “Your Majesty, the boldest cheats came first, believing that no questions would be asked. Yet thousands remain. We cannot examine them all before sunset.”

Lilimond thought awhile. Then he commanded the heralds to go into the square and proclaim:

“Let every person hear! Whosoever hath falsely claimed hunger, infirmity, widowhood, orphanhood, or other misfortune in order to gain royal gold shall be punished for deception. But whosoever is truly in need shall receive food, aid, and honest consideration.”

The trumpets sounded. The proclamation was cried once, twice, and three times.

For a moment the multitude stood still.

Then a curious change came over the square.

A lame man tucked his crutch beneath his arm and walked away. Two blind men recovered their sight and hurried after him. A woman with four borrowed children returned them to their astonished parents. Bandages vanished, bent backs straightened, and ragged cloaks were cast aside to reveal fur collars, good leather belts, silver buckles, and even velvet gowns.

Some slipped down alleys. Some climbed walls. Some departed with dignity, pretending they had merely come to watch. Others ran outright.

The tramp, tramp of arriving feet became the patter and clatter of retreat. Donkeys turned, carts creaked away, and dogs raced after their masters. Within half an hour, the square that had seemed packed beyond all counting was almost empty.

Only a small company remained near the fountain.

Lilimond descended from the throne and went among them himself.

There he found a mason whose arm had been crushed by a falling stone, and who could not work until it healed. There was a widow with three pale children; parish records proved that her husband had died of fever a fortnight before. There was an old soldier who had lost a leg defending the northern pass. There were two sisters whose cottage and spinning wheels had burned, a deaf woman abandoned by cruel relatives, and several aged laborers who had no family and no strength remaining.

The Prince questioned them gently, and Lord Ardwell verified each account. Not one wore hidden pearls; not one refused suitable work; not one asked for more than was needed.

To each Lilimond gave a gold piece. He also ordered food for the hungry, medicine for the sick, tools for those able to resume a trade, and places in the royal almshouses for the infirm.

When all had been served, the Lord Treasurer counted what had been spent.

“Your Majesty,” said he, smiling for the first time that day, “less than one quarter of the first coffer is gone.”

Lilimond looked at the six unopened coffers and then at the vast square where thousands had lately clamored.

He was silent a long while.

At last he returned to the throne room. The afternoon sun slanted through the high windows and made bars of gold upon the floor. King Florimund still sat in the plain chair, saying nothing. He had neither mocked the boy’s errors nor interfered with his commands, for he knew that certain lessons cannot be given like sweetmeats; they must be earned.

Lilimond removed the crown. His hair was flattened beneath it, and he looked weary beyond his twelve years.

“My father,” he said, “I believed that every rag covered misery, every complaint proved injustice, and every outstretched hand deserved gold. I thought your councilors hard-hearted because they asked questions before giving aid.”

“And what thinkest thou now?” asked the King.

“I think that questions may protect the needy from those who would steal their portion. Yet I would not become so suspicious that I refuse pity to all because many deceived me.”

King Florimund smiled.

“Thou hast learned in one day what some rulers fail to learn in fifty years.”

“I have learned also,” continued Lilimond, “that taxes maintain roads, guards, hospitals, bridges, and stores of grain. Gold in a treasury is not idle if it stands ready against famine or war. Yet, sire, perhaps we should send honest officers through the kingdom to seek those who are too weak or ashamed to beg.”

“That is wisely spoken,” said the King. “We shall do so.”

The Prince held out the crown.

“Sunset hath not yet come, but I return this willingly. It is too heavy for me today.”

King Florimund did not take it at once.

“Art thou certain? There remains nearly an hour of thy reign.”

“Of a surety, sire. I have commanded enough for one birthday. I would rather be your son until I am fit to be your successor.”

Then the King rose, placed the crown upon his own head, and embraced him before the assembled court.

“Let it be recorded,” he proclaimed, “that Lilimond ruled less than one day, spent less than one coffer, relieved every true petitioner who came before him, frightened a thousand rogues, discovered four pearls, six false orphans, eleven sham cripples, and one exceedingly foolish nobleman.”

At this the court laughed, and even Lilimond laughed with them.

That evening there was a feast in the Great Hall. The tables shone with silver, and the minstrels sang of the Day of the Vanishing Beggars. Yet before Lilimond tasted his birthday cake, he sent baskets of meat, bread, apples, and warm pudding to the poor families who had remained in the square.

For compassion had not left his heart; it had merely opened its eyes.

Years passed, as years do in kingdoms and cottages alike. Lilimond grew tall and grave, though he never lost his courtesy. He studied laws as diligently as he had once studied stars. He visited farms without announcing his coming, inspected parish houses, spoke with craftsmen, soldiers, widows, merchants, and laborers, and listened not only to what men said but also to what their lives revealed.

Master Borland continued to believe nearly every sad tale he heard, so Lilimond made him Royal Comforter, in which office his kindness did much good. Lord Ardwell remained Chamberlain and taught the Prince how accounts were kept, stores measured, claims tested, and relief distributed without waste or insult.

When King Florimund died at a venerable age, Lilimond became King in truth. The crown no longer slipped over his eyebrow, but he remembered always how heavy it had felt upon his twelfth birthday.

He ruled generously, though never carelessly. No starving person was turned from his gate; neither was idleness rewarded as though it were misfortune. Those unable to work received succor. Those able and willing were given work. Those who sought alms by fraud learned that mercy is not blindness, while officials who treated the unfortunate harshly learned that judgment is not cruelty.

Thus Valedore prospered through many peaceful years.

And if you ask whether it is better to give than to receive, the answer is surely yes. Yet the wise giver looks well at what he gives, to whom he gives it, and whether his gift will heal a sorrow or nourish a fault. Gold cast blindly into a crowd may be caught by the greediest hands; but kindness guided by judgment reaches those who need it most.

So remember the old rhyme:

> Beggars in tatters, beggars in tags,  
> Beggars who flourish in velvet and rags;  
> Give with a warm heart, but look ere you do—  
> For mercy is noblest when wisdom looks too.

The Last Lighthouse Keeper

On the morning the sea disappeared, Elias Vale was polishing the lighthouse lens.

He noticed the silence first.

For thirty-two years, the sea had spoken through the walls of the tower. It hissed over the rocks, struck the cliffs with hollow blows, and whispered beneath the floors at night. Elias had learned its moods as other men learned the moods of wives and children. He could tell a northern storm from a western gale by the pitch of the windows. He knew when the tide was rising by the tremor in his iron cup.

That morning, the cup stood perfectly still.

Elias lowered his cloth and listened.

Nothing.

He descended the spiral staircase, passed his narrow bedroom and the kitchen with its cold stove, and opened the lighthouse door.

The sea was gone.

Beyond the cliff lay a vast plain of wet sand, glistening beneath a pale sky. It stretched to the horizon, crossed by dark trenches and scattered pools. Fish twisted in the mud. Boats rested on their sides like toys abandoned by a careless child. Far away, where water had once met sky, something flashed in the rising sun.

Elias stood with one hand on the doorframe.

“Well,” he said at last. “That is unusual.”

He went back inside and made tea.

The wireless had stopped working three days earlier, but that was not unusual. Salt entered every machine eventually. The supply boat was due on Thursday, and its captain, Mara Venn, carried spare valves. Elias tried the wireless again while the kettle heated.

“Northwatch Light calling Port Mercy,” he said into the microphone. “Northwatch calling. The water appears to have withdrawn.”

Static breathed back at him.

He adjusted the frequency.

“The entire sea,” he added.

Still nothing.

At eighty-one, Elias had lost the habit of panic. Panic was useful when action remained possible. When a lamp caught fire, when a ship approached the reef in fog, when a man fell from the gallery, panic sharpened the limbs. But there was no lever he could pull to restore an ocean.

He drank his tea, filled a canvas bag, and walked down to the shore.

The exposed seabed smelled of salt, weeds, and old metal. The mud near the cliff swallowed his boots to the ankles, but farther out the ground became firm. Crabs scuttled through shallow channels. Eels writhed in shrinking pools. Elias carried as many stranded creatures as he could to deeper water, though he knew the pools themselves would soon vanish under the sun.

By noon, he had reached the wreck of the Saint Orison.

The ship had sunk before he was born. Local children knew the story: a winter gale, a drunken captain, forty-seven souls lost within sight of Northwatch. The wreck had remained beneath twelve fathoms of water for ninety years. Now its broken ribs rose from the sand, draped in green weed.

Elias stopped beside it.

A brass bell lay half buried near the bow. He scraped mud from its side and found the ship’s name engraved around the rim.

He lifted the bell and struck it with a piece of timber.

The note rolled across the empty seabed.

A second bell answered.

Elias frowned.

The answering sound came from the east, faint but unmistakable.

He climbed onto the wreck for a better view. Sunlight flashed again near the horizon. At first he took it for glass or metal. Then it moved.

Someone was walking toward him.

It took nearly an hour for the figure to arrive. She was a girl of perhaps fourteen, thin and brown-skinned, wearing a yellow coat far too large for her. A leather satchel hung from one shoulder. She carried a handbell.

“Are you the keeper?” she asked.

“I am.”

“Good.” She dropped onto a beam of the wreck and began pulling at her boots. “I was afraid you might be dead.”

“I’ve considered it from time to time.”

The girl looked up, uncertain whether he was joking.

Elias offered her his canteen. She drank greedily.

“What’s your name?” he asked.

“Lena.”

“Where did you come from, Lena?”

She pointed east.

There had never been anything east of Northwatch except water. The nearest island in that direction lay two hundred miles away.

“From a ship?”

“From the city.”

“What city?”

“The one under the sea.”

Elias regarded her in silence.

Lena reached into her satchel and removed a glass sphere the size of an apple. Something silver moved inside it, curling and uncurling like smoke.

“This is for you,” she said. “They said you would know what to do.”

“Who are they?”

“The people who remember the rain.”

She placed the sphere in his hands.

It was cold enough to hurt.

For a moment Elias saw his own face reflected in the glass: white beard, sunken cheeks, eyes faded by years of watching distant things. Then the silver smoke cleared, and another image appeared inside.

A woman stood at the edge of a harbor.

Elias nearly dropped the sphere.

Her name had been Anne. She had been dead for twenty-six years.

In the sphere she looked thirty again, with black hair tied at her neck. Wind pulled at her blue dress. She smiled at someone beyond the glass.

At him.

The image vanished.

Elias tightened his grip.

“Where did you get this?”

“Below,” Lena said. “In the Archive.”

He looked east, toward the flashes of light.

“What happened to the sea?”

“It went home.”

They walked back to the lighthouse together.

Lena moved quickly, skipping over channels and climbing the sides of exposed reefs. Elias followed more slowly, troubled by the vastness around him. Every familiar landmark had changed. The bell buoy stood crooked in the mud. The North Reef, once marked only by foam, rose like a black fortress. Caves opened in the cliff below the lighthouse, their entrances slick with weed.

By the time they reached the tower, the sun was setting.

The lens caught its final rays and cast a bright wheel over the dry horizon. Elias lit the lamp out of habit.

“There are no ships,” Lena said as she watched him check the flame.

“A lighthouse does not wait for ships before shining.”

“What does it shine for, then?”

“The possibility of them.”

She seemed to consider this seriously.

They ate canned beans and hard bread in the kitchen. Lena examined everything: the barometer, the oil clock, the logbooks lined along the shelves. She was especially interested in the rain gauge outside.

“Does rain still fall here?” she asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Real rain? From clouds?”

“Where else would it come from?”

She did not answer.

After supper, Elias set the glass sphere on the table between them.

“Tell me about the city.”

Lena cupped her hands around her tea.

“It was built before the drowning,” she said. “That’s what the teachers say. When the sea rose, the old people sealed the roofs and made air gardens. They thought they would stay below for ten years. Then a hundred years passed, and then five hundred.”

“Five hundred?”

“Maybe more. The clocks disagree.”

Elias glanced at the sphere.

“The surface hasn’t been flooded for five hundred years.”

“Not your surface.”

He waited.

Lena searched for the right words.

“The city is not under this sea. Not exactly. There are other seas folded inside this one. The Archive says the world is like a book that got wet. The pages stick together. Sometimes words bleed from one page to another.”

“That sounds inconvenient.”

“It is.”

“And now the sea has gone to one of these other pages?”

She nodded. “Ours.”

“Why?”

“Because we called it.”

Outside, the lighthouse beam swept over stranded rocks.

Lena explained that her city was dying. Its machines had begun to fail. Its reservoirs had turned bitter, and the sealed gardens produced less food each year. For generations, the Archivists had searched the folds between worlds. At last they found Northwatch Light.

“They saw the beam,” she said. “Light passes where people can’t.”

The city’s engineers built a machine to pull the sea through the fold. They expected a current, perhaps a river. Instead, they took everything.

“Can they send it back?” Elias asked.

“They won’t.”

“Can’t or won’t?”

“Both, maybe.”

He stood and walked to the window.

Under the moon, the empty seabed shone like bone.

Port Mercy depended on the sea. So did every village along the coast. There would be no fishing, no supply ships, no rain carried inland by ocean winds. Rivers would continue flowing for a while, pouring into the great hollow. Then they, too, might fail.

“How long?” he asked.

“Before what?”

“Before this world dies.”

Lena stared into her cup.

“The Archivists said longer than ours would have.”

Elias laughed once, without humor.

“Yes. I suppose that makes it fair.”

“I didn’t say it was fair.”

“No.”

“They sent me because of the sphere. The machine needs a guide to keep the fold open. A strong memory from both sides. They had one from our city, but they needed one from here.”

“And they chose Anne.”

“They didn’t choose her. You did.”

Elias turned.

Lena pointed to the logbooks.

“You wrote about her every day for forty years.”

The room seemed suddenly smaller.

The logbooks contained weather reports, lamp maintenance, passing vessels, supply inventories, and, hidden among these official details, the shape of his life. Anne visiting the tower in spring. Anne bringing a basket of pears. Anne laughing during a storm because the chimney had blown backward and filled the kitchen with soot. Anne leaving after their final argument. Anne’s marriage to a schoolmaster in Port Mercy. Anne’s illness, many years later. Anne’s funeral on a morning of hard rain.

He had never thought of the entries as a message.

“You read them?”

“Not me. The Archive did. The words made a path.”

“And the sphere?”

“It holds the path open.”

Elias sat across from her.

“What happens if I break it?”

Lena’s face tightened.

“The fold closes.”

“The sea returns?”

“Maybe.”

“And your city?”

“Drowns.”

He looked again at the silver smoke inside the sphere.

“Why did they send you to tell me this?”

“They didn’t.” Her voice dropped. “They told me to give you the sphere and say it was a gift.”

“Why didn’t you obey?”

Lena’s expression became angry, though whether at him or herself, Elias could not tell.

“Because I wanted to see rain.”

That night, neither of them slept.

Elias climbed to the lantern room and watched the beam turn. Lena remained below, sitting beside the sphere.

Near midnight, lights appeared on the seabed.

Hundreds of them moved out of the east in orderly rows. They were pale blue and floated a few feet above the ground. Beneath them marched people in dark suits with glass helmets. Long machines followed on jointed legs.

The city had come to secure its new shore.

Elias descended to find Lena waiting at the foot of the stairs.

“We have to go,” she said.

“Where?”

“To the fold. If you want to send the sea back, the sphere has to be broken there.”

“I thought breaking it here might work.”

“You asked what would happen. I said maybe.”

“And at the fold?”

“The Archive is certain.”

“That is less comforting than you think.”

She gave him a coil of rope and filled two packs with food, water, lamp oil, and blankets. Elias added his logbook and Anne’s brass compass. Before leaving, he extinguished the lighthouse lamp.

His hand rested on the valve.

It was the first time in thirty-two years that he had put out the light before dawn.

The journey east took two days.

They hid from the city patrols among reefs and wrecks. More people emerged from the fold each hour: engineers, soldiers, families carrying bundles. Some fell to their knees and touched the open air with bare hands. Others stared upward in terror, overwhelmed by the endless sky.

On the second afternoon, clouds gathered.

Lena noticed before Elias did.

She stopped beside the skeleton of a whale and pointed.

“Is that rain?”

“Not yet.”

The clouds were dark and low, moving from the north. Without the sea beneath them, Elias did not know whether they would strengthen or dissolve.

Lena walked backward, watching the sky until she tripped over a rib bone.

“Careful,” Elias said.

She laughed as she stood. “It’s bigger than I imagined.”

“What is?”

“Everything.”

Near sunset they reached the fold.

It hung in the air like a vertical river, a shimmering wall several miles wide. Through it Elias saw another world. Towers of bronze and glass rose from dark water. Domed roofs crowded narrow ridges of stone. Lamps glowed in submerged streets. Waves rushed through the opening and crashed into vast reservoirs while thousands of people watched from balconies.

A metal platform had been built before the fold. At its center stood a machine of turning rings.

Soldiers surrounded it.

Elias and Lena lay behind a ridge of coral.

“How close do we need to get?” he whispered.

“To the rings.”

“That is unfortunate.”

The glass sphere pulsed in his pack.

Across the open ground, one of the helmeted figures turned toward them.

Then another.

“Can they sense it?” Elias asked.

Lena was already running.

A blue light struck the ground beside her, throwing up sand. Elias followed as quickly as his legs allowed. Soldiers advanced from both sides, their weapons humming.

Lena reached the platform first. She climbed the rail and kicked one soldier in the knee. Elias swung his coil of rope at another, more from instinct than strategy. The weighted end wrapped around the soldier’s helmet. Elias pulled, and the man toppled backward.

Someone seized Elias from behind.

The sphere fell from his pack and rolled across the platform.

Every ring in the machine stopped.

Within the glass, Anne appeared once more.

She stood in the old lighthouse kitchen, flour on her hands. Elias remembered that day. They had tried to bake bread during a storm, and the loaf had emerged black outside and raw in the middle.

In the memory, Anne spoke, though no sound came from the sphere.

Lena dove for it.

A soldier caught her coat. She slipped out of it, leaving the yellow fabric in his hands, and closed both palms around the glass.

“Elias!” she shouted.

A deep vibration passed through the platform. The wall of water bent toward them.

Lena raised the sphere above her head.

Beyond the fold, alarms flashed red across the underwater city. People ran along balconies. Gates began to close over the reservoirs.

Elias saw children among them.

Thousands of children, perhaps tens of thousands. People who had never stolen anything, never built the machine, never agreed to trade one world for another. They had simply been born on the wrong side of a dying sea.

“Wait!” he cried.

Lena froze.

The soldiers did too.

An old woman emerged from the machine room. Unlike the others, she wore no helmet. Her skin had the gray pallor of someone who had never stood beneath a sun.

“You are Elias Vale,” she said.

He nodded.

“I am Archivist Senn. If you break the vessel, our barriers will fail. The returning water will crush the lower city.”

“If I don’t, my world becomes a desert.”

“We can share it.”

“You’ve taken the whole sea.”

“A miscalculation.”

“And your soldiers?”

“Another miscalculation.”

Lena still held the sphere above her head.

Thunder sounded.

Everyone looked up.

Rain struck the platform in one enormous drop. Then another.

Lena lowered the sphere.

The shower lasted only seconds, but her face changed as the water touched it. She closed her eyes and laughed. Around them, the people from the drowned city lifted their hands. Some screamed. One soldier removed his helmet and began to weep.

The rain darkened Elias’s sleeves.

He thought of Anne.

Not the young woman preserved in the sphere, but Anne in her final years, thin and sharp-eyed, sitting beside the hospital window. He had visited her once, though he had never written that in the logbook.

“You spent your life keeping a light for people who had already passed,” she had told him.

“I kept it for everyone.”

“No,” Anne had said. “You kept it because you were afraid that if you stopped, you would have to go somewhere new.”

At the time, he had been angry. Later, he understood.

A lighthouse did not command ships to remain at sea. It showed them where the rocks were. The rest was choice.

Elias turned to Archivist Senn.

“Can the fold be narrowed?”

She hesitated. “Yes.”

“Can the flow be controlled?”

“With time.”

“How much time?”

“A year. Perhaps two.”

“My people don’t have two years.”

Senn looked toward the wall of water.

“There may be another way. Your rivers still flow into the basin. Our machines could lift water from our reservoirs and return it as vapor.”

“Rain,” Lena said.

Senn nodded. “Enough to preserve the rivers and fields. Not enough to refill the sea.”

“And the coast?” Elias asked. “The fishing towns? The harbors?”

“Changed.”

It was a careful word, and a cruel one.

“Open the barriers,” Elias said. “Return enough water to cover the seabed. A shallow sea.”

“It would flood part of our city.”

“Then bring those people here.”

Senn looked toward the growing lines of refugees.

“Our atmosphere has weakened our lungs. Many of us cannot survive in this air.”

“We’ll build enclosed houses. You built a city under an ocean. I imagine you can manage windows.”

For the first time, the Archivist smiled.

Negotiations lasted nine days.

Representatives arrived from Port Mercy in wagons, having crossed the seabed after the lighthouse went dark. The mayor shouted for three hours. The fishermen shouted longer. Engineers from below produced maps. Farmers from above brought records of rivers and rainfall. No one was satisfied, which Elias considered evidence of a fair agreement.

The underwater city returned one-third of the sea.

It came through the fold slowly, guided into the deepest trenches. Water filled the old channels, lifted stranded boats, and covered the wreck of the Saint Orison. Islands rose where no islands had existed before. Port Mercy found itself ten miles inland, but a new river connected its harbor to the reduced ocean.

In exchange, the people of Northwatch accepted twelve thousand citizens from below.

They built glass-roofed settlements along the cliffs. The newcomers taught them to harvest salt from dry basins, grow food in sealed gardens, and shape metals that did not rust. The surface people taught them wind, birds, distances, and weather.

The first year was difficult.

The second was worse.

By the third, children from both worlds had invented games that could be played across the tidal flats, and adults reluctantly admitted that survival might be possible.

Elias returned to Northwatch Light.

The tower no longer stood at the edge of the sea. Water lay a mile away at high tide, farther at low tide. There was little need for a lighthouse, but he lit it every evening.

Lena stayed with him.

She grew herbs in the lantern room and filled the rain gauge with stones when the weather was too dry. She studied the lens, the lamp, and every volume of the log. When Elias’s hands began to shake, she took over the polishing.

Years later, on a spring night, he climbed the stairs for the last time.

Lena was waiting beside the lamp. She was twenty now, tall and strong, wearing a new yellow coat.

“The western marker is out,” she said. “I’ll repair it tomorrow.”

“Take the small boat. The current near the reef has changed.”

“I know.”

“Check the fuel line twice.”

“I always do.”

“And write it in the log.”

She rolled her eyes. “Yes, Elias.”

He sat beside the lens. Far below, the narrow sea reflected the moon. Lights glowed in the cliff settlements. Beyond them, the fold shone faintly on the horizon, no longer a wall but a silver thread.

“Do you regret it?” Lena asked.

“What?”

“Not breaking the sphere.”

The glass vessel stood on a shelf near the lamp. Its silver smoke had faded over the years. Anne appeared less often now, and never clearly.

Elias considered the question.

“There are things I regret,” he said. “That isn’t one of them.”

“If you had broken it, your sea would have come back.”

“Yes.”

“Everything might have stayed the way it was.”

“Nothing stays the way it was.”

Lena looked out through the glass.

A ship moved along the new channel. It had a shallow hull designed for the changed waters, and its sails were woven from fabric made in the city below. Children crowded its deck, pointing toward the lighthouse.

Elias stood with difficulty.

“Your watch,” he said.

Lena took her place beside the lamp.

He descended to his room, opened the final logbook, and wrote one last entry.

Weather calm. Visibility excellent. Western marker requires repair. Unfamiliar vessel passed north at 10:17, all lights correct.

He paused, listening.

The sea spoke softly in the distance. Not the old roar beneath the tower, but a quieter voice, changed by sandbars, channels, and new shores.

Elias added another line.

Keeper on duty.

Then he closed the book.

Above him, the great lens turned, carrying its beam across the water, the dry land, and the shining fold between worlds. It passed over ships that had not yet sailed and harbors that had not yet been built. It touched the roofs of the living and the graves of the dead.

And wherever it passed, people looked up.

The light did not promise that the sea would remain.

It did not promise safety, fairness, or a return to what had been.

It offered only a warning and a welcome:

Here are the rocks.

Here is the shore.

You are not alone.
